newsitem.title: UK: UK minister wards off criticism of strike laws.
newsitem.headline: UK minister wards off criticism of strike laws.

text.p: British Trade and Industry Secretary Ian Lang launched a preemptive strike on Wednesday against criticism by business leaders of plans to tighten curbs on trade unions.

The top employers' organisation, the Confederation of British Industry, holds a meeting later on Wednesday and is expected to deliver a cool response afterwards to the Conservative government's latest proposals to crack down on strikes.
Many British employers feel current labour legislation goes far enough. Any more stringent rules could jeopardise relations with workforces and confuse negotiations, they say.
"The views of the CBI are always listened to carefully by the government and we will consider them along with other views received during the period of consultation," Lang said.
"It is the responsibility of the government to lead and as with our previous reforms, we are confident that the CBI will be convinced of the importance of our proposals by seeing them work."

The latest plans, which go even further than the radical curbs introduced when Margaret Thatcher was prime minister, were first announced in November. They would allow trade unions to be sued if a strike causes "disproportionate or excessive effects".
Lang published the plans after strikes last summer by postal workers, the fire service and rail staff.
At the time, the CBI said its members doubted the legislation would be workable and many British employers see pitfalls in the new plans.

Speaking after the plans were first announced in November, Roger Young, director-general of the Institute of Management said they were unclear. "This legislation could mean employers and employees spending more time in court than around the negotiating table."
Lang said the CBI and other employers' organisations had traditionally been cautious about industrial relations reforms.
He said the CBI initially opposed the measures which became the core of the 1988 Employment Act -- the centrepiece of labour legislation introduced by Thatcher's government.
Under her successor, John Major, the Conservatives are searching for new radical ideas to attract voters back after 18 years in office without a break.
But time is ticking away to an election which must be held no later than May, and polls give the opposition Labour Party a lead of some 20 points.

Labour has said it would not repeal Thatcher's union laws. But it is committed to signing up for the European Union's Social Chapter, which standardises worker protection across the 15 nation bloc and is opposed by the Conservatives.
